passage:
Dear Kashish,

You asked why I left the party so suddenly on Saturday. I owe you an honest answer.

When someone slammed the door, my body froze. My heart was racing and I couldn't breathe properly. It's something that's happened since the flat fire two years ago. I told myself I was over it. I wasn't.

After Saturday, I finally booked an appointment with a therapist. We've had two sessions. She says what I'm feeling makes sense after what happened, and that there are ways to work through it. I've started practising slow breathing when it happens.

I'm telling you because you're my closest friend and I'm tired of making excuses. You don't have to fix anything. Just maybe don't slam doors near me. 😅

Arohi

qa.q: What happened to Arohi two years ago?
qa.a: Arohi lived through a flat fire.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel when the door slammed?
qa.a: Arohi felt panic: the body froze, the heart raced and breathing became hard.

qa.q: What steps is Arohi taking toward healing?
qa.a: Arohi booked a therapist, has had two sessions and is practising slow breathing when it happens.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Kashish might feel moved to be trusted this much, and understand the party moment differently now.

grounding: Shows a young woman recognising the lingering effects of a frightening experience and seeking therapy.

passage: This is hard to say out loud. When I was nineteen, a senior at my first workplace bullied me for a year. Shouting, humiliation in meetings. I left, got a better job, and thought it was behind me. But at twenty-five, every time my new manager called me into a room, my hands went cold. I'd over-apologise for everything. My friend Rekha said, 'Jahnavi, you're not like this with anyone else.' That stuck. I found a support group for people who'd faced workplace harassment. Hearing others describe the same fear made me cry the first night. Later I started counselling too. I'm not fully free of it. But I notice when it's the past talking, not the present.

qa.q: How long did the senior bully Jahnavi at the first workplace?
qa.a: The senior bullied Jahnavi for a year.

qa.q: What did Rekha's comment help Jahnavi realise?
qa.a: It helped Jahnavi realise that the fear around the new manager came from past bullying, not from what was happening now.

qa.q: What helped Jahnavi begin to heal?
qa.a: Joining a support group where others shared similar fears, and later starting counselling.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi's current manager be affected by Jahnavi's reactions?
qa.a: The manager might be confused by Jahnavi's over-apologising, without knowing it comes from past experiences.

grounding: Shows a young adult recognising lingering effects of past workplace bullying and seeking group and professional support.

passage: I'm Nirmala, Ojas's older sister. After the robbery at his shop, he seemed fine. He went back to work within a week. But I noticed he'd started checking the door locks three or four times every night. He stopped going to the market after dark, which he used to love. He snapped at our mother over small things. I didn't know if it was the robbery, and I didn't want to label him. So I just asked if he was sleeping. He admitted he wasn't. A few weeks later he told me he'd started seeing a counsellor, and that he'd joined a yoga class near his shop in the evenings. He still checks the locks. But he walked with me to the market last Friday.

qa.q: How many times did Ojas check the door locks every night?
qa.a: He checked them three or four times every night.

qa.q: What might Ojas's lock-checking and snapping suggest about his inner state?
qa.a: They suggest he still felt unsafe and on edge after the robbery, even though he seemed fine.

qa.q: How did Nirmala support Ojas without labelling him?
qa.a: She asked a simple, caring question about his sleep instead of diagnosing him, which opened a conversation.

qa.q: What is it like for Nirmala watching Ojas during this time?
qa.a: She is worried about his changes but unsure what's causing them, so she waits and asks gently.

grounding: Shows an observer noticing a young man's lingering reactions after a robbery and his steps toward healing.

passage: March: Six months after the bus crash she had walked away from, Ishita still froze whenever a horn blared. She took long auto routes to avoid the highway and told Pranav she was 'just being careful'. At night she woke with her heart pounding. April: Pranav found her sitting in the parked car, unable to start it, hands shaking. He didn't argue. He sat with her, then said, 'I think this is bigger than careful. Would you talk to someone?' She booked a counsellor the next week, hating that she needed to. May: The therapist had helped her notice what happened in her body when fear rose, and they practised slowly: first sitting in the car, then a quiet lane. On a Sunday she drove Pranav to the market, three kilometres, both hands tight on the wheel. She parked, breathed and laughed shakily. 'Again next week.'

qa.q: What did Ishita tell Pranav she was being?
qa.a: 'Just being careful'.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel about booking a counsellor?
qa.a: She hated that she needed help, which suggests some shame, even though she went.

qa.q: What made Pranav's approach helpful?
qa.a: He stayed calm, sat with her instead of arguing, named the problem gently and suggested professional support.

qa.q: What might that moment in the parked car have been like for Pranav?
qa.a: Worrying to see her shaking, yet he chose patience, which helped her feel safe enough to agree.

grounding: Shows a young woman recognising lingering fear after an accident and healing gradually with therapy and support.

passage: Eshaan, it's your Mridul Chacha. I heard you haven't been sleeping since the fire at your office. Let me tell you something I've told very few people. At twenty-four I was on a train that derailed near Itarsi. I wasn't badly hurt, but I saw things I won't describe. For a year I pretended I was fine. I snapped at your aunt, avoided trains, couldn't bear the sound of metal scraping. I thought men were supposed to just get over things. Then my hands started shaking at work. Your aunt found a counsellor at the district hospital, and I went, grumbling. Talking about it slowly, in that small room, helped more than I believed it could. Later I joined a Sunday walking group; nobody there knew, and that was restful too. The memory is still there, beta. It just doesn't drive anymore. Please let someone help you with this.

qa.q: Where did the train Mridul was on derail?
qa.a: Near Itarsi.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel during the year he pretended he was fine?
qa.a: He was distressed and ashamed of it, believing men were supposed to just get over things, so he hid it and snapped at people.

qa.q: What helped Mridul heal?
qa.a: Seeing a counsellor and talking about it slowly, along with a Sunday walking group that gave him calm company.

qa.q: How might Eshaan's aunt have experienced that year?
qa.a: Hurt by his snapping and worried when his hands began shaking, which is why she found him a counsellor.

grounding: An uncle recalls recognising the lingering effects of a frightening accident and healing through counselling and community.
